title: The practice of Medina
hookLine: Malik gave weight to the living practice of Medina's people

lines: A HADITH ON CALLING OFF A SALE.
cards: In the Muwatta's chapter on trade, Malik records a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: a buyer and a seller each keep the right to call off the deal as long as they haven't parted. Right under it, Malik adds a note.

Among us, he says, there's no fixed limit for this, and no practice of acting on it. He has just written the hadith down himself, carefully, with its chain. And in the same breath he says Medina doesn't do it that way.
That isn't carelessness. It's a method, and it's the heart of his school.

teach.b: The phrase is 'amal ahl al-Madinah, the practice of the people of Medina. Medina was where the Prophet lived his last years, where the companions prayed behind him and traded in his market.
Their children watched them, and their grandchildren watched their children.

teach.h: A WHOLE CITY AS A REPORT.
teach.b: So what Medina did, day after day, was itself a kind of report: not one person remembering one sentence, but a whole city carrying a way of life from parent to child.

teach.h: AL-LAYTH: THE COMPANIONS WENT ELSEWHERE TOO.
teach.b: For Malik, where the settled practice of Medina went one way and a single narrator's report went another, the practice could carry more weight.
The report might be true but limited, or later set aside, and the city's daily life would know. That's what the note under the trade hadith is doing. Then a friendly argument.

Al-Layth ibn Sa'd, a great scholar of Egypt, wrote Malik a letter of real respect and real disagreement. The companions, he said, didn't all stay in Medina. They went to Egypt, Syria and Iraq, and taught there too.

Medina's practice is precious, but it isn't the only living practice. Malik's school kept its method; the letter was preserved, and readers still point to it as scholars disagreeing well. Some knowledge lives on paper.
Some lives in how people stand, greet, trade and pray. Malik took the second kind seriously enough to build a school on it.

how: Maliki jurists treat the settled practice of the people of Medina as strong evidence of the Prophet's sunnah, at times preferring it over a report carried by a single narrator.

games.q: what does “the practice of medina” mean?
o: a list of hadith that only Medina's scholars knew
the settled way Medina's people lived, a living report
the Prophet's rules for trading in Medina's market

games.q: the practice of Medina — tap the pairs.
p: no practice of acting on it here

s: Malik left out the hadith his city didn't act on
he recorded the trade hadith in the Muwatta, then noted Medina's practice beneath it.
al-Layth ibn Sa'd wrote to Malik with respect and disagreement
the companions taught in Egypt, Syria and Iraq too, he argued.
for Malik, a single report always outweighed the city's practice
where the settled practice of Medina went another way, it could carry more weight.

games.q: you're Malik. a sound-looking hadith says buyer and seller may call off a deal until they part, but Medina doesn't practice it. what do you write?
o: leave the hadith out of your book.
record the hadith, and note that Medina's practice differs.
change Medina's practice to match the hadith.
games.why: he records it, with its chain, and adds: among us there's no fixed limit for this and no practice of acting on it.

practice: Bring to mind a group whose ways you learned by watching, not reading: a family at holidays, a restaurant kitchen, a mosque, a team, a choir.
Pick one thing you learned there that nobody ever wrote down, how to set the table, when to stay quiet, who gets served first, and notice that you carry it now, the way Medina carried its practice.
If you pray, you can remember the people who taught you without meaning to.

wordCard.voice: The practice of Medina. 'Amal ahl al-Madinah: the settled way the people of Medina lived, which Malik treated as a living report of the Prophet's way. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the practice of the people of Medina; 'amal means action, what is done.

carryVoice: Your line: the living practice. A whole city can carry what one narrator remembers. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Muwatta Malik, Kitab al-Buyu' (the option of buyer and seller until they part, with Malik's comment)
